english.html: gument from the one to the other is by so much the better as the things have more nearly between them the fitting proportion; whence a rule in our law is drawn by our interpreters, that in things which are alike the argument from the one to the other is easy, as also in things unlike it is very difficult <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Wherefore, returning to the matter begun, between the prisoner and the sisters of Martin Guerre (of whom two were almost of like age with the same prisoner, and the other two came near it), the argument from likeness was without difficulty more proper than from a little child, such as the said Sanxi was, aged thirteen years only, to a man of thirty-five, such as the said prisoner was.

notes.citation: Digest 6.1 (De rei vindicatione), l. In rem, § Item quaecumque (cf. D. 6.1.23.3, Paul, on accessions joined to another thing; fragment identified with fair confidence, paragraph unverified); Digest 37.1 (De bonorum possessionibus), l. Sed cum patrono (fragment not identified)

notes.gloss: The glossators' rule drawn from these texts: in similibus facilis, in dissimilibus difficilis est argumentatio — argument from like to like is easy, from unlike to unlike hard. The `⟨alt⟩` at item quacun-⟨alt:itam quæcun-⟩que is taken as either: each reading has one wrong letter, and both resolve to Item quaecumque. The P. stands for the paragraph sign.

english.html: And as to saying that the said prisoner does not know how to speak the language of the Basques, the truth of the fact supplies the answer: for it results from the inquiries that Martin Guerre was brought a little child from his native land, and that he was then only two years old, or thereabouts

A child in Latin is called INFANS until the age of seven years a, as it were unable to speak (quasi nescius fari), that is to say, as not knowing how to speak: because, being in this tender age, he can scarcely yet untie his tongue to pronounce the words distinctly. Whence Chrysippus said that children who are already beginning to babble and to pronounce some words may be said almost to speak, but in truth they say nothing, nor speak at all. Thus one must not be astonished if, in the matter of which we treat, the prisoner, who had been brought very small, and at the age of little more than two years, from the Basque country, had not retained the language, which he never understood nor ever knew how to speak.

notes.citation: Accursius (Accurſe), the Gloss on Code 6.30 (De iure deliberandi), l. Si infanti (cf. C. 6.30.18, Theodosius and Valentinian, on the acquisition of an inheritance by an infans; number unverified); the Gloss on the Liber Sextus, VI 1.9 (De temporibus ordinationum et qualitate ordinandorum), c. Nullus (chapter number unverified)
notes.original: Accurſe en la l ſi infanti. C. de iur. de li bro. Gloſe au c. nullus de tẽpor. ordinand. au vj.
notes.gloss: Both glosses define infans as a child under seven, qui fari non potest; the print's de li bro is de li[be]r[ando], De iure deliberandi, with a reflow gap.
